topic: Introduction to Health Insurance and the Health System in India
t: Under the Constitution of India, 'public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries' is a subject in the:
e: Public health, hospitals and dispensaries fall under Entry 6 of the State List, which is why health service delivery is primarily a State responsibility while the Centre funds national programmes.

topic: Introduction to Health Insurance and the Health System in India
t: The Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 is chiefly associated with which concept?
o: Primary health care as the key to 'Health for All'
Mandatory social health insurance for workers
Creation of national drug price control
e: Alma-Ata declared primary health care as the route to 'Health for All by 2000'; it did not deal with social insurance, privatisation or drug pricing.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Under SDG indicator 3.8.2, a household is said to incur 'catastrophic' health spending when out-of-pocket health expenditure exceeds what share of total household consumption or income?
e: SDG 3.8.2 uses thresholds of 10% and 25% of household budget, with 10% being the primary measure; 40% of 'capacity to pay' is an older WHO measure, not a share of total consumption.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY provides a health cover of how much per eligible family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation?
e: PM-JAY, launched in September 2018, offers ₹5 lakh per family per year on a floater basis with no cap on family size; ₹30,000 was the limit under the earlier RSBY.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: The Employees' State Insurance Scheme currently covers employees whose monthly wages do not exceed:
e: The ESI wage ceiling was raised to ₹21,000 per month from January 2017 (₹25,000 for persons with disability); ₹15,000 was the earlier ceiling.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: Which of the following is a 'benefit' (fixed-sum) health product rather than an indemnity product?
e: A hospital cash policy pays a fixed amount per day of hospitalisation regardless of actual expenses, so it is a benefit product; the others reimburse actual hospital bills up to the sum insured.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: Mr Arora holds a base policy of ₹3 lakh and a super top-up of ₹10 lakh with an aggregate deductible of ₹3 lakh. In one year he has three hospitalisations costing ₹2 lakh, ₹1.5 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh. How much will the super top-up pay in total?
e: Total claims are ₹6 lakh; a super top-up applies the deductible to aggregate annual claims, so it pays ₹6 lakh − ₹3 lakh = ₹3 lakh. An ordinary top-up would have paid nothing because no single claim exceeded ₹3 lakh.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: A critical illness policy commonly stipulates a 'survival period'. This means:
o: The insured must have held the policy for at least 5 years
The insured must survive a stated number of days after diagnosis for the benefit to be payable
The benefit is paid in instalments over the insured's remaining life
The policy lapses if the insured survives the illness
e: Survival periods (typically 30 days) ensure the lump sum is paid to a living insured for treatment and lifestyle costs, distinguishing the product from life cover.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: The standard product Arogya Sanjeevani Policy carries a mandatory co-payment on every claim of:
e: Arogya Sanjeevani has a fixed 5% co-pay on all admissible claims, along with room rent capped at 2% of sum insured and ICU at 5% of sum insured.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under Section 41 of the Insurance Act, 1938, offering a rebate of premium as an inducement to buy a health policy is:
o: Prohibited and punishable with a penalty of up to ₹10 lakh
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 41 bars rebating by any person; the 2015 amendment raised the penalty to up to ₹10 lakh.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: 'Domiciliary hospitalisation' in a health policy refers to:
o: Treatment in a hospital located in the insured's home town
Medical treatment at home for a condition that would normally require hospitalisation, because the patient cannot be moved or no bed is available
OPD consultation at a network clinic
Treatment of a family member living in the same house
e: Domiciliary hospitalisation covers in-home treatment of a hospitalisable illness when the patient cannot be shifted or beds are unavailable, usually subject to a minimum duration and specified exclusions.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: Mrs Iyer's policy of ₹5 lakh has a 100% restoration benefit. She claims ₹5 lakh for a cardiac surgery in June and ₹2 lakh for the same illness in September of the same policy year. The policy restores the sum insured only for unrelated illnesses. The September claim is:
o: Payable in full from the restored sum insured
Payable to the extent of ₹1 lakh only
Not payable, because restoration does not apply to the same illness
Payable only after a fresh 30-day waiting period
e: Many restoration clauses exclude claims for the same illness or the same person already claimed in that year; since the base sum insured is exhausted and restoration does not apply, nothing is payable.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: 'Adverse selection' in health insurance means the tendency of:
o: Persons with higher-than-average risk of illness to seek insurance more actively than healthy persons
Insurers to decline proposals from senior citizens
Insured persons to over-use services once covered
Agents to sell policies with the highest commission
e: Adverse selection arises when those who expect to claim are more likely to buy cover, distorting the pool; over-use after purchase is moral hazard, not adverse selection.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: An insured who opts for a costlier private room and extra diagnostic tests simply because 'insurance will pay' is an example of:
e: Moral hazard is the change in behaviour once a person is insured, leading to higher utilisation; co-payments and sub-limits are the underwriting tools used to control it.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: As per IRDAI's standard definition, a 'pre-existing disease' is a condition that was diagnosed, or for which medical advice or treatment was recommended, within how many months before the first policy issued by the insurer?
e: The standard definition uses a 36-month look-back prior to the first policy; the 48-month figure relates to the earlier maximum PED waiting period, which was reduced to 36 months in 2024.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: A proposer weighs 80 kg and is 1.60 m tall. His Body Mass Index is approximately:
e: BMI = weight ÷ height² = 80 ÷ (1.6 × 1.6) = 80 ÷ 2.56 = 31.25, which falls in the obese category (BMI ≥ 30) and would normally attract underwriting attention or loading.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: Which of the following is NOT a standard underwriting decision available to a health underwriter on a sub-standard proposal?
o: Accept with a specific permanent exclusion
Postpone the decision for a defined period
Accept now and cancel unilaterally after the first claim
e: Underwriters may accept, load, exclude, postpone or decline at the proposal stage; a policy once issued cannot be cancelled by the insurer merely because a claim arises, except for established fraud or non-disclosure.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: A group health policy for 2,000 employees is priced mainly on the group's own past claims rather than on each member's health status. This approach is called:
e: Large groups are experience-rated using their own claims history; community rating charges the same premium regardless of history, and medical underwriting assesses individuals.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: A pure premium of ₹4,000 is to be loaded for expenses of 25% and profit of 5% of gross premium. The gross premium is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). When loadings are expressed as a percentage of gross premium, gross = pure ÷ (1 − 0.25 − 0.05) = 4,000 ÷ 0.70 = ₹5,714 (approx.).

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Under IRDAI's standard definition, a 'hospital' in a town with a population of less than 10 lakh must have at least how many in-patient beds?
e: The standard definition requires at least 10 in-patient beds in towns with population below 10 lakh and 15 beds elsewhere, along with round-the-clock nursing, a qualified medical practitioner and an operation theatre.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: 'Day care treatment' as defined in standard health policy wordings refers to medical or surgical treatment that:
o: Is taken in a hospital or day care centre in less than 24 hours because of technological advancement, and would otherwise have required hospitalisation
Is taken during daytime hours only
Is given at the patient's residence during the day
e: Day care treatment is defined by the under-24-hour stay made possible by technology (e.g. cataract, dialysis, chemotherapy); OPD treatment is specifically excluded from the definition.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: A policy allows room rent up to ₹4,000 per day. The insured occupies a room costing ₹8,000 per day and the total admissible hospital bill (excluding medicines and consumables) is ₹2,00,000. Applying proportionate deduction, the payable amount on this portion is:
e: The eligible proportion is 4,000 ÷ 8,000 = 50%, so associated medical expenses are reduced to ₹1,00,000. Proportionate deduction applies only to room-linked expenses, not to pharmacy or consumables under IRDAI norms.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Under IRDAI's guidelines on standardisation of exclusions, which of the following can no longer be excluded from a health insurance policy?
o: Treatment for mental illness and psychological disorders
Cosmetic surgery not necessitated by injury
Participation in hazardous or adventure sports as a professional
e: The 2019 guidelines, in line with the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, prohibit exclusion of mental illness; cosmetic surgery, professional hazardous sports and unproven treatments remain permitted standard exclusions.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: 'Pre-hospitalisation medical expenses' are admissible under a policy only if:
o: They were incurred in the same hospital as the admission
They relate to the same condition for which hospitalisation was required and the in-patient claim is admissible
e: Pre-hospitalisation expenses must be for the same illness and the in-patient claim must be accepted; they need not be at the same hospital and expenses after discharge are post-hospitalisation.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Under the IRDAI Master Circular on health insurance (2024), after how many months of continuous coverage can an insurer no longer contest a claim on grounds of non-disclosure or misrepresentation, except for established fraud?
e: The moratorium period was reduced from 8 years (96 months) to 60 months in 2024; after it, claims can be contested only for proven fraud or for permanent exclusions.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: A portfolio of 50,000 insured lives generated 4,000 claims in a year with an average claim size of ₹45,000. The pure (risk) premium per life is:
e: Pure premium = claim frequency × average severity = (4,000 ÷ 50,000) × ₹45,000 = 0.08 × 45,000 = ₹3,600; expenses, profit and contingency loadings are added on top to arrive at the office premium.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: 'IBNR' in health insurance reserving stands for claims that:
o: Have been reported and fully paid
Have been rejected but may be reopened
Have occurred but have not yet been reported to the insurer as on the valuation date
e: Incurred But Not Reported claims have happened but intimation is pending; an estimate must be reserved because health claims are often intimated after discharge.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: An insurer's health portfolio earned premium of ₹400 crore in a year. Claims paid were ₹300 crore, outstanding claims rose by ₹20 crore and IBNR rose by ₹10 crore. The incurred claims ratio is:
e: Incurred claims = paid + change in outstanding + change in IBNR = 300 + 20 + 10 = ₹330 crore; ICR = 330 ÷ 400 = 82.5%.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: A family's annual consumption expenditure is ₹2,40,000. In the year, it spent ₹36,000 out of pocket on hospitalisation. Under the 10% threshold definition, the family's health spending is:
o: Not catastrophic, as it is below 10%
Catastrophic, as it is 15% of consumption
Catastrophic only if the family is below the poverty line
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). 36,000 ÷ 2,40,000 = 15%, which exceeds the 10% threshold used in SDG 3.8.2, so the spending is catastrophic regardless of poverty status.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The ICD classification maintained by WHO is used by Indian health insurers mainly to:
o: Grade hospitals by number of beds
Fix maximum tariff for surgical procedures
Code diagnoses uniformly so that claims data can be analysed
e: The International Classification of Diseases provides standard diagnosis codes, enabling consistent recording, pricing analysis and data sharing (e.g. with IIB); it does not fix tariffs or grade hospitals.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The reserve held for the portion of premium already received that relates to the unexpired period of policies in force is called the:
e: Unearned premium reserve (or unexpired risk reserve) represents premium not yet earned; outstanding and IBNER reserves relate to claims already reported, and catastrophe reserves are for extreme events.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: 'Health insurance business' as defined in Section 2(6C) of the Insurance Act, 1938 (as amended in 2015) includes:
o: Sickness and medical expense benefits, assured benefits, long-term care, travel and personal accident cover
Life insurance with a critical illness rider only
e: The 2015 amendment defined health insurance broadly, covering indemnity and benefit contracts, long-term care, travel and personal accident; this allowed health to be treated as a distinct class of business.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The minimum paid-up equity capital required to register a stand-alone health insurance company in India is:
e: The Insurance Act prescribes ₹100 crore for life, general and stand-alone health insurers and ₹200 crore for reinsurers.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) framework of 2024, the free-look period available on a health insurance policy is:
o: 15 days from receipt of the policy, for all policies
15 days for electronic and 30 days for physical policies
Available only for policies of three years or more
30 days from the date of receipt of the policy document
e: From 2024, IRDAI extended the free-look period to 30 days from receipt of the policy for all policies, replacing the earlier 15-day (30-day for distance marketing) rule.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Section 64VB of the Insurance Act, 1938 requires that:
o: No risk shall be assumed unless the premium is received in advance
Every policy must carry a nomination
Claims must be paid within 30 days
e: Section 64VB mandates receipt of premium before commencement of risk; rebating is dealt with under Section 41 and claim timelines are set by regulations, not this section.

topic: IRDAI – regulator
t: The minimum paid-up equity capital required to start a life or general insurance company in India is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹100 crore for a direct insurer; ₹200 crore for a reinsurer (Section 6 of the Insurance Act).

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The grace period for renewal of an annual health insurance policy, during which continuity benefits are protected, is:
e: A 30-day grace period applies to annual-premium health policies (15 days where premium is paid monthly); cover for claims during the grace period is not automatic unless renewed.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Which of the following statements about entry age in individual health insurance products in India is correct after IRDAI's 2024 changes?
o: No person above 65 years can buy a fresh policy
Insurers must not impose any maximum entry age, so products should be available across all ages
Entry is restricted to persons below 75 years
Senior citizens can buy only government schemes
e: In April 2024 IRDAI removed the 65-year cap on entry age; insurers must offer products for all age groups, though they may design products for specific segments.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under IRDAI's regulatory framework, a life insurance company may offer health insurance products that are:
o: Benefit-based only (e.g. critical illness, hospital cash) and not indemnity-based
Both indemnity and benefit-based without restriction
e: Life insurers are restricted to benefit-based health products; indemnity-based (expense-reimbursing) products may be offered only by general and stand-alone health insurers.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: Under the 2024 Master Circular on health insurance, an insurer must decide on a cashless pre-authorisation request within:
e: Cashless authorisation must be decided within 1 hour of the request and final discharge authorisation within 3 hours; delay beyond 3 hours makes any extra hospital charges the insurer's cost.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: The maximum value of a complaint that an Insurance Ombudsman can entertain under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules (as amended in 2021) is:
e: The limit was raised from ₹30 lakh to ₹50 lakh in 2021; complaints must be filed within one year of the insurer's final reply.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: The 'Customer Information Sheet' (CIS) that must accompany every health policy is intended to:
o: Replace the policy document as the legal contract
Summarise key features such as coverage, exclusions, waiting periods and claim procedure in simple language
e: The CIS, in the revised format mandated from 1 January 2024, gives a plain-language summary of the policy; the policy wording remains the contract.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: If an insurer delays settlement of a health claim beyond the regulatory timeline, it must pay interest to the policyholder at:
o: Bank rate prevailing at the beginning of the financial year plus 2%
No interest is payable; only a penalty to IRDAI
e: Policyholder protection norms require interest at the bank rate plus 2% from the date the claim became due, in addition to any regulatory action.

topic: Health Insurance Fraud
t: A hospital bills a simple appendectomy as a complicated laparoscopic procedure with higher reimbursement. This type of provider fraud is known as:
e: Upcoding is billing a more expensive procedure than was performed; phantom billing bills services never rendered, and unbundling splits a package into separately billed components.

topic: Health Insurance Fraud
t: The 'fraud triangle' used in fraud risk management consists of:
e: Cressey's fraud triangle explains that fraud occurs when financial pressure, an opportunity and a self-justifying rationalisation coincide.

topic: IRDAI – regulator
t: The control level of solvency ratio that every insurer must maintain is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Available solvency margin must be at least 150% of the required solvency margin; falling below triggers IRDAI action.

topic: Health Insurance Fraud
t: A claim is received 25 days after policy inception for a 5-day hospitalisation for a chronic kidney condition, with bills from a hospital that has no listed registration number. Which action is most appropriate for the claims team?
o: Settle quickly to meet turnaround time norms
Refer for investigation given multiple red flags, while keeping the claimant informed
e: Early claims for chronic conditions and unregistered providers are classic red flags; the correct response is a documented investigation within timelines, not summary rejection or unverified payment.

topic: Reinsurance
t: A reinsurance arrangement that reimburses the insurer when the annual loss ratio of its health portfolio exceeds an agreed percentage is called:
e: Stop-loss covers the aggregate result of a portfolio above a threshold loss ratio, making it well suited to high-frequency, low-severity health business.

topic: Reinsurance
t: A health insurer has a 40% quota share treaty. On a policy with premium ₹20,000 and a claim of ₹1,50,000, the reinsurer's share of the claim is:
e: Under quota share the reinsurer takes the agreed fixed percentage of every premium and claim: 40% × ₹1,50,000 = ₹60,000; the insurer retains ₹90,000.

topic: Reinsurance
t: The key difference between facultative and treaty reinsurance is that facultative reinsurance:
o: Covers an entire class of business automatically
Is available only from GIC Re
Is negotiated risk by risk, with the reinsurer free to accept or decline each one
e: Facultative cover is placed individually for a specific risk, whereas a treaty obliges the reinsurer to accept all risks of a defined class; either can be proportional or non-proportional.
